messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajiv stepped off the bus at 6:47 AM, the same time he had for forty-two years, though he had not worked in the warehouse for over a decade. He was seventy-nine now, a wiry South Asian man with a salt-and-pepper beard he kept trimmed short, still wearing the steel-toed boots he could not bring himself to throw away. The bus stop was two blocks from the old loading dock, and every morning he stood there for a few minutes, watching the trucks reverse into their bays, listening to the hydraulic hiss of the brakes. It was the only place that felt real to him anymore.

The war had been in Vietnam, though he rarely said the word aloud. He had been nineteen, a recent immigrant from Punjab, drafted before he could vote. One night in the Mekong Delta, monsoon rain had turned the rice paddies into a black mirror, and the mortar round had landed so close that the blast wave had lifted him off his feet and slammed him against a dike. He had lain there for hours, pinned under a dead comrade, listening to the rain and the screaming. He never learned the man's name. What stayed with him, what he could still smell in the fabric of his own coat on humid mornings, was the wet earth and the copper taste of blood and the feeling of being absolutely certain that he was already dead.

Decades later, in the warehouse, the loading dock had been his sanctuary. The forklifts whining, the cardboard dust, the fluorescent hum — none of it bothered him. But the first time a truck's air brakes released their pressure with a sharp, percussive hiss, he had dropped to his knees behind a pallet of canned tomatoes, his heart pounding so hard he thought it would crack his ribs. The foreman had laughed, called him a jumpy old man. Rajiv had laughed too, then gone home and sat in his dark apartment for three days.

He had come to believe, in the years since, that he was broken in a way that could not be fixed. The world was full of hidden explosives — a car backfiring, a child's balloon popping, the clatter of a dropped metal tray in a diner. Each time, the same thing happened: his chest would seize, his vision would narrow to a tunnel, and he would be back in that paddy, the rain on his face, the weight of the dead man pressing him into the mud. He had learned to scan every room before entering it, looking for exits, for cover, for the shapes of things that could hide a threat. The grocery store was the worst — too many aisles, too many corners. He shopped at 6 AM, when the store was empty, and he always walked the perimeter first, checking the fire exits.

His daughter, Priya, had stopped calling. She had been the one to find him, years ago, cowering behind the couch during a thunderstorm, and she had said, "Dad, you need help," and he had said, "I'm fine," and they had both known it was a lie, but neither of them had the words to push through it. After the divorce, his wife had told him he was impossible to live with, that he slept with a knife under his pillow and woke up swinging. She had been right. He had not meant to hurt her. He had not meant to do any of it.

Last week, his neighbor's son had bought a motorcycle, and the first time the boy started the engine in the driveway, Rajiv had thrown himself flat on the kitchen floor, the tile cold against his cheek, and he had lain there for twenty minutes, waiting for the explosion that never came. When he finally got up, his hands were shaking so badly he could not hold the kettle. He had looked at his reflection in the window — an old man in a thin t-shirt, his face gray with fear — and he had thought, *This is not living. This is just waiting to die.*

He had called the VA clinic the next morning. The woman on the phone had asked him what was wrong, and he had said, "I don't know how to stop being afraid." She had scheduled him for an intake. He had hung up and sat in the dark, his back against the wall, facing the door, listening to the silence, waiting for the sound that would send him back to the mud.
